cards.definition_en: An event that harms, or threatens to harm, the security of systems or data and needs a planned response.
examples: The team declared an incident when the database server started sending data to an unknown address.
Every incident is recorded in the ticket system.
common_mistakes: Treating every alert as an incident: many alerts turn out to be harmless.
Writing 'incedent'.

cards.definition_en: Quickly judging which alerts or incidents matter most, so the most serious ones are handled first.
examples: During triage the analyst decided that the alert was a false alarm.
Good triage keeps the team from drowning in low-priority alerts.
common_mistakes: Starting a deep investigation before checking how serious the alert is.
Thinking it is only a medical term.

cards.definition_en: Actions that stop an incident from spreading, for example by cutting an infected computer off from the network.
examples: Containment started with disconnecting the infected laptops from the network.
Wiping the machines too early would have destroyed evidence before containment was complete.
common_mistakes: Switching a compromised server off immediately and losing the evidence in memory.
Mixing it up with eradication, which removes the cause.

cards.definition_en: Removing the cause of an incident from the environment, such as malware, rogue accounts or the flaw that was used.
examples: Eradication included deleting the attacker's accounts and closing the hole in the web server.
Without proper eradication the intruder may come back.
common_mistakes: Restoring systems before the cause has been removed.
Spelling it 'eradiction'.

cards.definition_en: Bringing affected systems back to normal operation and watching them closely to be sure the problem is gone.
examples: Recovery began with restoring the servers from clean backups.
The team monitored the systems for a week after recovery.
common_mistakes: Declaring the incident closed right after systems start working.
Restoring from a backup that may already contain the infection.

cards.definition_en: A meeting and report after an incident that explains what happened and what should change, usually without blaming individuals.
examples: The post-mortem showed that the alert was ignored because of too much noise.
Everyone attended the post-mortem and agreed on three improvements.
common_mistakes: Using the post-mortem to find someone to blame.
Skipping it when the incident was short.

cards.definition_en: The underlying reason for a problem which, once fixed, prevents the same problem from happening again.
examples: The root cause was a password that had never been changed after an employee left.
Fixing the symptom without finding the root cause leads to repeated incidents.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the first visible reason instead of asking why again.
Confusing the root cause with the trigger of the incident.

cards.definition_en: A piece of evidence, such as a file fingerprint, an address or a domain name, that suggests a system has been broken into.
collocations: search for an indicator of compromise
examples: The analyst searched all computers for the indicator of compromise from the report.
A strange outgoing connection can be an indicator of compromise.
common_mistakes: Thinking one indicator proves a breach: it only suggests it.
Treating old indicators as always valid, though attackers change addresses quickly.

cards.definition_en: Collecting and examining electronic evidence carefully, so that it can be trusted and used to understand an incident or in court.
examples: Digital forensics showed which files the attacker had opened.
A copy of the disk was made for digital forensics before any repair.
common_mistakes: Working on the original disk instead of a copy.
Using 'forensic' as a noun for the whole field.

cards.definition_en: A written record of everyone who handled a piece of evidence and when, proving that it was not altered.
examples: The laptop was sealed and signed over to keep the chain of custody intact.
A gap in the chain of custody can make evidence useless in court.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with a supply chain.
Forgetting to record who held the device overnight.

cards.definition_en: A written, step-by-step procedure that tells the team what to do for a certain type of incident.
examples: The ransomware playbook says to isolate the machine first.
A playbook saves time because decisions are made before the crisis.
common_mistakes: Treating the playbook as a rigid rule that forbids thinking.
Never testing the playbook before a real incident.

cards.definition_en: Passing a problem to more senior or specialized people when it is too serious or too complex for the current handlers.
examples: The first-line analyst started an escalation when customer data was involved.
A clear escalation path tells everyone whom to call at night.
common_mistakes: Waiting too long because escalating feels like admitting failure.
Mixing it up with 'escalator' or with making a conflict worse.

cards.definition_en: A system that gathers log messages from many sources, compares them and raises an alert when they show something suspicious.
examples: The SIEM raised an alert after fifty failed logins from one address.
Logs from firewalls and servers flow into the SIEM.
common_mistakes: Thinking a SIEM stops attacks by itself: it detects and reports.
Sending logs to the SIEM without anyone reading its alerts.

cards.definition_en: A tool that watches network traffic or computers for signs of attack and raises an alert, without blocking anything itself.
examples: The intrusion detection system noticed a scan of the internal network.
An intrusion detection system only warns; an intrusion prevention system can block.
common_mistakes: Thinking it blocks attacks: that is the job of a prevention system.
Ignoring alerts because of many false positives instead of tuning the rules.

cards.definition_en: Actively searching a network for hidden intruders instead of waiting for an alert.
examples: Threat hunting found an old backdoor that no alert had caught.
Analysts start threat hunting from a theory about how an attacker might behave.
common_mistakes: Thinking hunting means only reading the SIEM alerts.
Doing it without a clear question to answer.

cards.definition_en: A kind of harmful software that locks or encrypts a victim's files and demands money to give them back.
examples: The hospital restored its systems from backups instead of paying the ransom demanded by the ransomware.
A ransomware attack often begins with a phishing email.
common_mistakes: Believing that paying always returns the data.
Keeping the only backup on a network drive that the ransomware can also encrypt.

cards.definition_en: Secretly copying or sending data out of an organization without permission.
examples: Large uploads at night were a sign of data exfiltration.
The attacker used the web server for data exfiltration over many days.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with data loss from a broken disk.
Spelling it 'exfiltrating' as a noun.

cards.definition_en: The way an attacker who has entered one computer moves on to other computers inside the network.
examples: Network segmentation makes lateral movement harder.
The attacker used stolen credentials for lateral movement to the file server.
common_mistakes: Thinking an attacker stops at the first compromised computer.
Confusing it with privilege escalation, which is about getting higher rights.

cards.definition_en: Techniques that let an attacker keep access to a system after a restart or a password change.
examples: The malware created a scheduled task for persistence.
Eradication must include removing every persistence mechanism.
common_mistakes: Using the word only in its everyday sense of being determined.
Cleaning the malware file but leaving the scheduled task that restarts it.

cards.definition_en: Steps taken to reduce the damage or the likelihood of a risk when it cannot be removed completely.
examples: Blocking the address was a quick mitigation until the patch arrived.
The report lists the mitigation for each risk.
common_mistakes: Treating a mitigation as a full fix.
Spelling it 'mitigaton'.

cards.definition_en: A rating of how serious an incident or vulnerability is, based on its impact and how easily it can be exploited.
examples: The team assigned the highest severity because customer data was exposed.
The severity can change when new facts appear.
common_mistakes: Mixing up severity (how bad) with priority (how soon to act).
Setting the severity once and never reviewing it.

cards.definition_en: A practice session in which the team talks through how it would handle an imagined incident, without touching real systems.
examples: During the tabletop exercise the team discovered that nobody knew the manager's phone number.
A tabletop exercise is cheaper than a full technical drill.
common_mistakes: Thinking it involves attacking real servers.
Practicing only with the technical team and leaving out management.

cards.definition_en: A flaw that the software maker does not know about yet, so no fix exists, or an attack that uses such a flaw.
examples: Attackers used a zero-day to break into the mail server before a patch existed.
Monitoring helps to notice a zero-day even when no signature is available.
common_mistakes: Thinking zero-day means a flaw that was found on the first day of the year.
Believing that updates alone protect against it.

cards.definition_en: An attack that makes a service unavailable to real users, usually by overloading it with traffic or requests.
examples: A denial of service attack flooded the shop with fake requests on the busiest day.
Rate limiting reduces the effect of a simple denial of service.
common_mistakes: Thinking it steals data: it only blocks access.
Writing 'denial of services'.

cards.definition_en: Isolating a suspicious file or device so that it cannot affect other systems while it is examined.
examples: The antivirus moved the suspicious attachment into quarantine.
The infected laptop stayed in quarantine until the analysts finished their work.
common_mistakes: Deleting a file from quarantine without checking it.
Spelling it 'quarentine'.
